title: Containers: images and registries
objective: Find, inspect and retrieve container images with podman and skopeo.

questions.q: What is Podman?
options: A daemonless tool to run and manage OCI containers, largely drop-in compatible with Docker
questions.explain: Podman needs no background daemon and can run rootless, which the RHCSA exam favors.

questions.q: Which file controls which registries Podman searches for unqualified image names?
questions.explain: The unqualified-search-registries list decides where a bare name like "nginx" is looked up.

questions.q: What does `skopeo inspect docker://registry.access.redhat.com/ubi9/ubi` do?
options: Shows an image's metadata (layers, labels, digest) WITHOUT pulling it
questions.explain: skopeo works on remote images directly, so you can inspect before downloading.

questions.q: A fully qualified image name looks like:
questions.explain: It is registry/namespace/name:tag. Using the full name avoids ambiguity.

questions.q: Where does a rootless user's pulled images get stored?
questions.explain: Rootful storage is /var/lib/containers/storage; each rootless user has their own.

questions.q: What does an image "tag" represent?
options: A specific version/label of an image (e.g. :latest, :9.3)
questions.explain: Pin a real version tag for reproducibility; :latest can change under you.

questions.q: Search the configured registries for images named "ubi9".
questions.explain: Results depend on your registries.conf search list.

questions.q: Pull the Red Hat UBI 9 base image.
questions.explain: Confirm afterward with `podman images`.

questions.q: List the container images stored locally.
questions.explain: Shows repository, tag, image ID, and size.

questions.q: Inspect a remote image's metadata without downloading it.
questions.explain: Add `--config` to see the runtime config; great for checking before a pull.

labs.title: Configure a registry and pull (exam-style)
labs.scenario: Make registry.access.redhat.com a searchable registry, search for ubi9, pull the ubi image, and confirm it is stored locally.
steps: # ensure "registry.access.redhat.com" is in the list (edit if needed)
verify: podman images | grep ubi9

labs.title: Inspect an image before and after pulling
labs.scenario: Compare inspecting an image remotely with skopeo versus locally with podman.
verify: you can read the image's labels and digest both ways

labs.title: Log in to a registry
labs.scenario: Log in to a container registry with your credentials, then confirm the stored login.
verify: podman login --get-login registry.redhat.io shows your user

labs.title: Copy an image between locations with skopeo
labs.scenario: Use skopeo to copy an image into local container storage without running it.
verify: the image appears in local storage under the new name

title: Containers: running and managing
objective: Run, list, stop, start, inspect and remove containers.

questions.q: Which command runs a container in the background and names it?
questions.explain: -d detaches (daemon-like); --name gives it a stable name.

questions.q: What does `podman ps` show by default?
questions.explain: Add -a to include stopped containers.

questions.q: How do you get an interactive shell inside a running container named web?
questions.explain: -i keeps stdin open, -t allocates a terminal.

questions.q: What does `-p 8080:80` do in podman run?
options: Maps host port 8080 to container port 80
questions.explain: Reach the service at http://host:8080.

questions.q: Which command shows a container's logs?
questions.explain: Add -f to follow the logs live.

questions.q: A stopped container still exists until you:
options: Remove it with podman rm (or run with --rm to auto-remove on exit)
questions.explain: `podman ps -a` lists stopped containers taking up space.

questions.q: What does `podman inspect web` provide?
options: Detailed JSON about the container (mounts, network, env, state)
questions.explain: Filter with `--format '{{.State.Status}}'` for one field.

questions.q: Run an nginx container in the background named web, mapping host port 8080 to 80.
questions.explain: Test it with `curl http://localhost:8080`.

questions.q: List all containers including stopped ones.
questions.explain: Running-only is just `podman ps`.

questions.q: Stop the running container named web.
questions.explain: Start it again with `podman start web`; restart with `podman restart web`.

questions.q: Remove the container named web (it must be stopped first, or use force).
questions.explain: -f stops and removes in one step.

labs.title: Full container lifecycle (exam-style)
labs.scenario: Run a named nginx container with a port mapping, verify it serves, exec in to look around, read its logs, stop it, start it, then remove it.
steps: podman stop web && podman start web
verify: podman ps -a shows no "web" container remaining

labs.title: Run a one-shot command in a container
labs.scenario: Run a UBI container that prints the OS release, then removes itself automatically.
verify: the command output appears and `podman ps -a` shows no leftover container

labs.title: Set environment and inspect it
labs.scenario: Run a container with a custom environment variable and confirm it is set inside.
steps: podman run -d --name envtest -e GREETING=hello registry.access.redhat.com/ubi9/ubi sleep 300
verify: the container sees GREETING=hello

labs.title: Interactive container
labs.scenario: Start an interactive UBI container, create a file inside it, exit, and observe the container has stopped.
verify: you understand the container stops when its main process exits

title: Containers: persistent storage and environment
objective: Attach host storage to containers with correct SELinux labels.

questions.q: Why does data written inside a container usually disappear when the container is removed?
options: The container's writable layer is ephemeral; only mounted volumes persist
questions.explain: Persistent data must live on a mounted host directory or named volume.

questions.q: Which podman option bind-mounts a host directory into a container?
questions.explain: -p is for ports; -v (or --volume) is for storage.

questions.q: On an SELinux-enforcing host, what does the :Z suffix on a volume do?
options: Relabels the host directory with a private container context so the container can access it
questions.explain: Without :Z (or :z), SELinux typically denies the container access to the host files.

questions.q: The difference between :z and :Z on a volume is:
options: :z labels it shared among containers; :Z labels it private to one container
questions.explain: Use :Z when only one container should use the directory.

questions.q: A "named volume" (podman volume create) differs from a bind mount because it:
options: Is managed by Podman under its storage, not a specific host path you choose
questions.explain: Bind mounts point at an exact host directory; named volumes are Podman-managed.

questions.q: Which permanent SELinux type should a host directory served by a container have?
questions.explain: Set it with semanage fcontext + restorecon so it survives a relabel (better than relying on :Z alone).

questions.q: Run a container mounting host /srv/web into /usr/share/nginx/html with a private SELinux relabel.
questions.explain: :Z relabels /srv/web to container_file_t for this container.

questions.q: Create a Podman-managed named volume called appdata.
questions.explain: Inspect it with `podman volume inspect appdata`; list with `podman volume ls`.

questions.q: Permanently label the host directory /srv/web for container use.
questions.explain: Then apply it with `restorecon -Rv /srv/web`.

labs.title: Persistent web content (exam-style)
labs.scenario: Serve content from host /srv/web through an nginx container so the page survives removing and recreating the container.
verify: curl http://localhost:8080 still shows "Hello from the host"

labs.title: Use a named volume
labs.scenario: Create a named volume, mount it in a container, write data, remove the container, and confirm the data persists in a new container.
steps: podman run --rm -v appdata:/data registry.access.redhat.com/ubi9/ubi bash -c 'echo persisted > /data/file.txt'
verify: the second container reads "persisted" written by the first

labs.title: Prove the SELinux label matters
labs.scenario: Mount a host dir WITHOUT :Z and observe the denial, then fix it with the label.
verify: curl http://localhost:8081 now serves the file

labs.title: Inspect a container's mounts
labs.scenario: Run a container with a bind mount and use inspect to confirm the mount source, destination and mode.
verify: you can read the mount details from inspect

title: Containers: building images from a Containerfile
objective: Write a Containerfile and build a custom image with podman build.

questions.q: What is a Containerfile?
options: A text file of instructions (FROM, RUN, COPY, CMD...) that defines how to build an image
questions.explain: It is the same format as a Dockerfile; Podman reads either name.

questions.q: The first instruction in a Containerfile is normally:
questions.explain: FROM sets the base image every later layer builds on.

questions.q: What is the difference between CMD and ENTRYPOINT?
options: ENTRYPOINT sets the fixed executable; CMD sets default arguments that are easy to override
questions.explain: A common pattern is ENTRYPOINT for the program and CMD for default args.

questions.q: RUN vs CMD in a Containerfile:
options: RUN executes during the BUILD (creating a layer); CMD runs when the container STARTS
RUN runs at start, CMD at build
questions.explain: Use RUN to install software; use CMD/ENTRYPOINT to define the runtime process.

questions.q: Which instruction copies files from your build context into the image?
questions.explain: COPY src dest; ADD can also fetch URLs/untar, but COPY is preferred for clarity.

questions.q: What does `podman build -t myapp:1.0 .` do?
options: Builds an image tagged myapp:1.0 from the Containerfile in the current directory
questions.explain: The trailing "." is the build context directory.

questions.q: Build an image tagged webapp:1.0 from the Containerfile in the current directory.
questions.explain: Confirm with `podman images | grep webapp`.

questions.q: Show the history/layers of the image webapp:1.0.
questions.explain: Each Containerfile instruction that changes the filesystem creates a layer.

questions.q: Which instruction sets an environment variable baked into the image?
questions.explain: ENV values are present at both later build steps and runtime.

labs.title: Build a custom web image (exam-style)
labs.scenario: Write a Containerfile based on UBI that installs a tiny web server or copies an index page, then build and run it.
steps: RUN dnf install -y httpd && dnf clean all
verify: curl -s http://localhost:8080 shows "Purva's container"

labs.title: Understand build layers
labs.scenario: Build an image, then use history and inspect to see its layers and configured command.
verify: you can list the layers and the default command

labs.title: ENV and CMD in practice
labs.scenario: Write a small Containerfile that sets an ENV variable and a CMD that prints it, then build and run to confirm.
verify: the container prints "Hello Purva"

labs.title: Tag and re-tag an image
labs.scenario: Build an image, add a second tag, and push (or save) it.
verify: both tags exist and the image is saved to a tarball

title: Containers: running as a systemd service
objective: Configure a rootless container to start automatically at boot with Quadlet.

questions.q: On RHEL 10, the current recommended way to run a container under systemd is:
options: A Quadlet unit (a .container file) that systemd generates a service from
podman generate systemd (now the older method)
questions.explain: Quadlet files live in ~/.config/containers/systemd/ (rootless) or /etc/containers/systemd/ (rootful).

questions.q: For a ROOTLESS container service to keep running after the user logs out (and start at boot), you must:
options: Enable lingering for that user with loginctl enable-linger <user>
questions.explain: Without linger, user services stop when the user's last session ends.

questions.q: A Quadlet file named webapp.container produces a systemd service called:
questions.explain: systemctl --user start webapp.service starts it; the name matches the file's base name.

questions.q: Which command must you run after creating or editing a Quadlet unit?
options: systemctl --user daemon-reload (rootless) so systemd regenerates the service
questions.explain: For rootful units in /etc/containers/systemd/, use `systemctl daemon-reload`.

questions.q: In a Quadlet [Container] section, which key maps a host port to the container?
questions.explain: Other common keys: Image=, Volume=, Environment=.

questions.q: The older `podman generate systemd --new --name web --files` command:
options: Generates a systemd unit file for an existing container (still seen on RHEL 9)
questions.explain: RHEL 10 favors Quadlet, but knowing generate systemd is still useful.

questions.q: Enable lingering for the current user so rootless services run at boot.
questions.explain: Check with `loginctl show-user $USER | grep Linger`.

questions.q: Reload the user systemd manager after adding a Quadlet unit.
questions.explain: Then `systemctl --user start <name>.service`.

questions.q: Enable and start a rootless user service named webapp now.
questions.explain: For Quadlet-generated services, `enable` may be implicit via [Install]; start is what matters.

labs.title: Rootless container as a service with Quadlet (exam-style)
labs.scenario: As a regular user, create a Quadlet unit that runs an nginx container on port 8080, enable lingering, and make it start at boot.
verify: systemctl --user status webapp.service is active; curl http://localhost:8080 works; survives reboot

labs.title: Persistent storage in a Quadlet unit
labs.scenario: Extend your Quadlet unit to serve content from host ~/webroot with the correct SELinux label.
verify: curl http://localhost:8080 shows "quadlet page" and it persists across restarts

labs.title: Legacy method: generate systemd
labs.scenario: For an existing running container, generate a systemd unit the older way and enable it as a user service.
verify: systemctl --user is-active container-legacyweb.service is active

labs.title: Verify a service survives reboot
labs.scenario: Confirm your rootless container service comes back after a reboot (thanks to linger).
steps: systemctl --user is-enabled webapp.service 2>/dev/null || echo "started via Quadlet"
verify: the container is running again after the reboot without you starting it

title: Containers: management, pods and troubleshooting
objective: Consolidate container skills: pods, auto-update, cleanup and troubleshooting.

questions.q: What is a Podman "pod"?
options: A group of containers that share networking (like a Kubernetes pod)
questions.explain: Containers in a pod reach each other on localhost and share published ports.

questions.q: Which command removes all stopped containers, unused images and networks to reclaim space?
questions.explain: Add -a to also remove unused images; it prompts before deleting.

questions.q: `podman stats` shows:
options: Live CPU, memory and I/O usage per container
questions.explain: Useful for spotting a runaway container.

questions.q: How do you copy a file from a running container to the host?
questions.explain: `podman cp` works in both directions, like docker cp.

questions.q: A container keeps exiting immediately. The best first troubleshooting step is:
options: Check its logs with podman logs <name>
questions.explain: The logs usually show the crash reason (bad config, missing file, permission).

questions.q: `podman inspect` with `--format` is used to:
options: Extract a specific field (like the IP or state) from a container's JSON
questions.explain: e.g. `--format '{{.NetworkSettings.IPAddress}}'`.

questions.q: What does `podman auto-update` do (with a label on the container)?
options: Checks the registry and restarts the container if a newer image is available
questions.explain: It pairs with a systemd timer for hands-off image updates.

questions.q: Create a pod named webpod that publishes host port 8080.
questions.explain: Then run containers with `--pod webpod`.

questions.q: Show live resource usage for all running containers.
questions.explain: --no-stream prints one snapshot instead of a live view.

questions.q: Copy /etc/os-release out of the running container "web" to the current directory.
questions.explain: Works while the container is running or stopped.

labs.title: Build a two-container pod (exam-plus)
labs.scenario: Create a pod publishing port 8080, run a web container inside it, and confirm it is reachable and that both share the pod's network.
verify: podman ps shows the container in webpod and the site responds

labs.title: Troubleshoot a crashing container
labs.scenario: Deliberately run a container with a bad command, read the logs to find why it exits, then fix it.
steps: podman logs broken                # shows "no such file or directory"
verify: podman ps shows "fixed" running; you diagnosed the failure from logs

labs.title: Clean up container resources
labs.scenario: List everything using space, then prune stopped containers and unused images safely.
steps: podman ps -a; podman images; podman volume ls
verify: podman system df shows reclaimed space

labs.title: Extract and edit a config from a container
labs.scenario: Copy a config file out of a running container, inspect the container's IP, and copy an edited file back in.
verify: the file is copied both ways and you retrieved the container IP
